name: @voxgig/sdkgen-infrapack
description: Infrastructure-provider targets for the Voxgig SDK Generator: Seneca provider.
author: Richard Rodger (http://richardrodger.com)

scripts.test: node tools/comment-gate.cjs && node tools/dep-gate.cjs && node --enable-source-maps --test test/*.test.js
scripts.reset: npm run clean && npm i && npm run build && npm test
scripts.repo-tag: REPO_VERSION=`node -e "console.log(require('./package').version)"` && echo TAG: v$REPO_VERSION && git commit -a -m v$REPO_VERSION && git push && git tag v$REPO_VERSION && git push --tags;
scripts.repo-publish: npm run clean && npm i && npm run repo-publish-quick
scripts.repo-publish-quick: npm run build && npm run test && npm run repo-tag && npm publish --registry https://registry.npmjs.org --access=public

_peer_comment: A MIGRATED TARGET INHERITS SDKGEN'S PEERS AS ITS OWN. These components
import @voxgig/sdkgen and @voxgig/apidef BY NAME, which resolved silently
while the target lived in the bundled scaffold beside sdkgen's own
node_modules. Out here they have to be declared, or the components fail
to type-check for the author and fail to resolve for anyone who installs
this package without sdkgen's peers present.
Peers rather than dependencies: a consumer necessarily has these already,
via sdkgen, and a second copy at a different version is the one outcome
worth preventing.
NOT @seneca/maintain, AND NOT ANY OTHER SENECA PACKAGE. The migration
guide's candidate-check grep prints @seneca/maintain for this target, and
declaring it here would be wrong: the hit is inside the template literal
in Extras that WRITES the generated provider's test file. The Seneca
packages are dependencies of the generated provider, declared in
.sdk/model/target/seneca-provider.aon's `deps` block, and a consumer of
THIS package has no reason to supply any of them. The grep cannot tell an
import from an emitted string; expect that from any target generating a
Node package.
No @voxgig/struct either — haskell needs it, this target does not.
The apidef floor MATCHES SDKGEN'S OWN peer range rather than being
chosen here. A consumer satisfies this package through sdkgen, so a
looser range would only let npm resolve an apidef that sdkgen itself
rejects — a package that installs and then fails to generate.
THE SDKGEN FLOOR IS THE OLDEST PUBLISHED VERSION THIS SUITE IS RUN
AGAINST. `peerDependencies` below is where the suite's copy lives, and
the `floor` lane in .github/workflows/build.yml reads it from there and
reinstalls at it, so the claim is enforced rather than asserted. This
prose deliberately does not repeat the version: a second copy of a
version number is the copy that goes stale.
There IS a second copy, and it is not this one — `engines.sdkgen` in
sdkgen-package.json, which a consumer's `package add` reads and no lane
reads. Nothing asserts the two agree, so raising the floor means editing
both.
Not the oldest that might work: a floor nobody tests is the shape of the
old >=3.5.0, which accepted versions where a target's components install
and then die at generation on a missing export — this target calls
`pointSegments`, which sdkgen first exported in 4.8.0. So raising the
floor is a deliberate act and lowering it is a claim about what has been
run; the lane is what settles either.
This is a SEPARATE REPOSITORY, so there is no `file:` path back to the
generator: the dependency is the published package, and that is the
point. It makes this package's CI the thing that catches an sdkgen
release breaking a packaged target.
@types/node IS REQUIRED, not incidental: these components import
`node:path` and read `__dirname`. Inside the sdkgen checkout they
hoisted from the generator's own devDependencies; standing alone that
hoist is gone and the type-check lane fails.
memfs IS REQUIRED TOO, and nothing here imports it. `generateInto` in
@voxgig/sdkgen/testkit requires it at run time while sdkgen declares it
only as a devDependency, so it does not reach a consumer and the kit
throws `needs memfs — add it as a devDependency`. It is pinned EXACTLY,
matching sdkgen's own pin: this is the kit's own dependency borrowed
across a package boundary, so tracking what the kit is developed against
beats resolving newest independently of it. An unused-dependency scan
will flag it; it is load-bearing.
